claims.text: A binary relation on a finite lottery space admits a surreal expected‑utility representation iff it satisfies completeness, transitivity, continuity*, and independence*.

claims.text: Completeness: for any two lotteries x and y, either x is at least as good as y or y is at least as good as x.
claims.quote: 1. Completeness: ∀x, y ∈X, either x ⪯y or y ⪯x.

claims.text: Transitivity: if x ⪯ y and y ⪯ z then x ⪯ z.
claims.quote: 2. Transitivity: ∀x, y, z ∈X, if x ⪯y and y ⪯z, then x ⪯z.

claims.text: Continuity*: if x ⪯ y ⪯ z then there exists a surreal probability p in ⋆[0,1] such that the mixture px+(1−p)z is indifferent to y.
claims.quote: 3. Continuity⋆: ∀x, y, z ∈X, if x ⪯y ⪯z, then there exist a surreal p ∈⋆[0, 1] such that px + (1 −p)z ∼y.

claims.text: Independence*: for any lotteries x, y, z and any surreal p in (0,1], x ⪯ y iff the mixture px+(1−p)z is at most as good as py+(1−p)z.
claims.quote: 4. Independence⋆: ∀x, y, z ∈X, ∀p ∈⋆(0, 1], x ⪯y if and only if px + (1 −p)z ⪯ py + (1 −p)z.

claims.text: The core of the wager is that fearing the error of rejecting true Christianity is greater than fearing the error of believing a false Christianity.
claims.quote: I should be much more afraid of being mistaken and then finding out that Christianity is true than of being mistaken in believing it to be true.

claims.text: Pascal argues that the gains from believing in God are infinitely greater than the losses from not believing.
claims.quote: Pascal points out what the gambler has to gain and allows him to weigh the gains against the losses, all the while making sure that the gains are infinitely more than the losses.

claims.text: The Wager can be reformulated with love for God and fear of injustice instead of fear of Hell, without changing its structure.

claims.text: Pascal states that in the wager, winning yields everything while losing yields nothing.
claims.quote: if you win, you win everything, if you lose, you lose nothing.

claims.text: Pascal presents the expected value of believing as an infinitely happy life, making the gamble reasonable.
claims.quote: Pascal offers the Expected Value as an infinitely happy life to be won when choosing God.

claims.text: Christianity promises eternal happiness, so believers gain everything and lose nothing; atheism offers only nothingness at death.
claims.quote: Christianity offers eternal happiness, therefore you gain everything and lose nothing, while if you do not believe you gain nothing and you lose everything; in atheism there is no eternal bliss, only nothingness at death.

claims.text: If Christianity is true, believers will know they were right after death, whereas atheists who are wrong will be aware of their error.

claims.text: A development of William James’s position can satisfy the conditions of possibility and ethical acceptability for a doxastic venture model.

claims.text: The objection does not apply to certain framework principles presupposed by theistic belief and practice.

claims.quote: A fiducial venture model seems to have at least one important advantage over the doxastic venture model. Because it does not endorse believing beyond what the evidence warrants, it apparently offers better prospects for reconciling faith with reason.

claims.text: The fiducial venture model may struggle to fully account for the venturesomeness of faith.
claims.quote: A disadvantage with a fiducial venture model of faith, however, is that it may have difficulty accounting fully for faith’s venturesomeness.

claims.text: If evidential defences of theistic belief are circular, doxastic venture may be needed to break the circle.

claims.text: James says it is morally permissible to believe beyond evidence on a passional basis only if (1) the question cannot be decided intellectually and (2) the question is a genuine option.

claims.text: An option is momentous when which hypothesis is adopted significantly affects the person’s actions or life.

arguments.title: Framework principles demand realist belief

atoms.A: A framework principle is a claim whose truth is presupposed by an entire system of beliefs and practices
atoms.B: Any attempt to rationally ground a framework principle's truth is circular
atoms.D: Accepting a limited framework's principles can be a Jamesian genuine option that is evidentially undecidable
atoms.E: Resolving an evidentially undecidable framework principle can reasonably be a matter of believingly accepting a passional inclination to believe it true
atoms.F: A Jamesian defence of doxastic venture succeeds
atoms.G: A reasonable choice of a framework principle can be a matter of accepting a belief about reality
atoms.H: Some framework principles must be understood realistically rather than non-realistically

arguments.missing_premise: If reasonably resolving an evidentially undecidable framework principle can be a matter of believingly accepting a passional inclination to believe it true, then a reasonable choice of a framework principle can be a matter of accepting a belief about reality. [E -> G]
